people.label: Charles E. Schumer
people.sub: Senate Majority Leader (2021-2025); sponsor, UAP Disclosure Act
people.narrative: Schumer is the author of the only piece of United States legislation ever drafted on the explicit premise that the Federal Government holds recovered non-human technology and has hidden it. On 13 July 2023, as Senate Majority Leader, he submitted S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226, the FY2024 NDAA, for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich; its text was printed in the Congressional Record at Vol. 169 No. 120, pages S2953-S2959. The amendment carried a legal definition of 'non-human intelligence,' a legal definition of 'legacy program' reaching private contractors and academic institutions, a nine-member Records Review Board appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, and — at Section __10(a), later Section 9010(a) of Division G of the engrossed bill — a command that 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' The Senate passed S. 2226 carrying that division on 27 July 2023. By the time the conference product was signed on 22 December 2023 the Review Board, the eminent domain clause, the Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and the $20,000,000 authorization were gone; only Sections 1841-1843 survived. Schumer framed the effort as inheriting Harry Reid's project, telling reporters he was 'honored to carry on the legacy of my mentor and dear friend Harry Reid,' and after the gutting said it was 'really an outrage the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board.' He re-filed the full text through Rounds as S.Amdt. 2610 in July 2024. It never got a vote.
people.tierRationale: Named sponsor of record on the only federal bill text that legislates over recovered non-human material; his amendment is the single most-cited primary document in the modern disclosure record.

people.label: Mike Rounds
people.sub: R-SD; SASC and SSCI; lead Republican on the UAPDA
people.narrative: Rounds is the Republican half of the UAPDA and, unlike Schumer, he has never stopped filing it. He was an original cosponsor of S.Amdt. 797 on 13 July 2023. When the provision was gutted in conference he took over as lead sponsor: on 11 July 2024 the full text, eminent domain clause intact, was submitted to the FY2025 NDAA as S.Amdt. 2610, captioned 'Mr. ROUNDS (for himself and Mr. Schumer),' and printed in the Congressional Record for that day. It was ordered to lie on the table and was never called up; the FY2025 NDAA, P.L. 118-159, signed 23 December 2024, contains no UAP disclosure division at all. Rounds sits on both the Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, the two panels that would have to be rolled to move this, and his position on the inside is what makes his persistence significant rather than symbolic. As of 2026 he is still at it: in his own newsletter for the week of 22-28 June 2026 he wrote, 'On Thursday, I spoke at the 2026 Disclosure Symposium, where I discussed the future of the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) Disclosure Act. I am once again cosponsoring as an amendment to this year's National Defense Authorization Act.' That FY2027 NDAA, S. 4784, was reported by the Armed Services Committee in June 2026 containing no UAP provisions of any kind, which means the vehicle Rounds is aiming at has again been built without a place for him.
people.tierRationale: Original cosponsor in 2023, lead sponsor in 2024, still filing in 2026, and seated on both committees of jurisdiction — the continuity of the legislative effort runs through him, not Schumer.

people.label: Kirsten E. Gillibrand
people.sub: D-NY; author of Sec. 1683, FY2022 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373)
people.narrative: Gillibrand built the statutory machine that everything else in this domain hangs off. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, P.L. 117-81, signed 27 December 2021 and codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, ordered the Secretary of Defense and the DNI to stand up a permanent office to absorb the UAP Task Force, to force reporting into a centralized repository, and to report to Congress. It was restated a year later by Section 6802 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023, enacted inside P.L. 117-263 on 23 December 2022, which named the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, put its Director reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI, and at subsection (j) demanded a written historical record report on the United States Government's dealings with UAP built from intelligence community records, oral history interviews and interviews of current and former officials. In February 2023 Gillibrand and Rubio led sixteen senators demanding full funding for AARO, arguing it 'provides the opportunity to integrate and resolve threats and hazards to the U.S., while also offering increased transparency.' She was an original cosponsor of S.Amdt. 797 in July 2023. Her posture is different from Schumer's: she legislates the plumbing, not the seizure. It is her plumbing — Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA — that survived when Schumer's Review Board did not, and it is that surviving language she invoked on 8 May 2026 when the administration began releasing files, saying the government must 'finally meet its legal obligation to the American people.'
people.tierRationale: Author of the underlying statutory authority (50 U.S.C. 3373) that every later UAP provision cross-references; her language is the only part of the architecture that has never been stripped.

people.sub: R-FL; SSCI Vice Chair 2021-2025; cosponsor of the UAPDA; left Senate Jan 2025
people.narrative: Rubio matters here because of what he had access to. people.label: Michael R. Turner
people.sub: R-OH; Chairman, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (2023-2025)
people.narrative: Turner is the name most consistently attached to the killing of the UAP Disclosure Act. As Chairman of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence through the FY2024 NDAA conference he held one of the four corner positions on the intelligence side of the negotiation, and the two provisions reported to have been his targets — the eminent domain clause and the Review Board's subpoena power — are precisely the two the enacted statute does not contain. Attorney Daniel Sheehan, who lobbied the conference directly, has stated on the record that 'Mike Turner first attacked those two elements,' demanding the eminent domain provision and the subpoena power be taken out. Turner had already positioned himself against the underlying testimony: after the 26 July 2023 House Oversight hearing he said the striking thing was that 'repeatedly over and over again, the whistleblowers had to say, actually, I don't have any knowledge.' The documentary result is not in dispute even if the attribution is journalistic: the Senate passed Sections 9001-9015 on 27 July 2023; the conference product signed 22 December 2023 contains Sections 1841, 1842 and 1843 only. Sections 9007 through 9011 — Review Board, Board personnel, review of records, eminent domain, court-sealed materials — have no enacted counterpart. Under the board's premise this is the single most consequential act of concealment in the modern legislative record, and it was performed by a committee chairman with access to the underlying compartments.
people.tierRationale: Named by a direct participant as the person who demanded removal of the two enforcement provisions, and the enacted text matches that account exactly.

people.label: Mike D. Rogers
people.sub: R-AL; Chairman, House Armed Services Committee (2023- )
people.narrative: Rogers chaired the House Armed Services Committee through the FY2024 NDAA conference and, as chairman of the committee of primary jurisdiction over the bill, was one of the four principals whose sign-off the conference report required. He is named alongside Turner as leading the effort to eliminate or significantly alter the UAP Disclosure Act. His institutional interest is structural rather than personal: the UAPDA as passed by the Senate would have created an independent agency outside the Armed Services Committee's oversight, with authority to compel production from the Department of Defense and from its contractors, and to seize material from those contractors by eminent domain. Every enforcement mechanism in the Senate text that would have operated outside the armed services and intelligence committee structure was removed; the mechanisms that survived — a records collection at the National Archives, a review by agency heads, and postponement decisions made by the original classification authority — leave the existing committee architecture untouched. The FY2024 NDAA also confirms this in a second place: Sec. 1687, which Rogers's committee produced, disciplines unreported UAP special access programs by cutting off funds, but routes the remedy to 'the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership' rather than to any outside board.
people.tierRationale: Named in contemporaneous reporting as co-leading the removal and held the chairmanship that made the removal possible, but no direct quotation or document ties him personally to a specific section.

people.label: Mark R. Warner
people.sub: D-VA; SSCI Chairman 2021-2025; author of the IAA contractor turn-in
people.narrative: Warner is the author of the provision that goes furthest of anything Congress has ever passed toward acknowledging privately held recovered material. On 13 July 2023 he submitted S.Amdt. 666 to S. 2226, the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024, which became Division M of the engrossed bill. Its Section 1102 does three things no other enacted or passed text does. It cuts off all funds for UAP activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' that has not been 'formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified' to Congress, and then enumerates exactly what it means: recruiting and securing personnel whose mission is 'capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft'; analysing such craft to determine 'material composition, method of manufacture, origin'; 'reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology'; and 'any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Second, it orders any person under contract with the Government holding such material to notify the Director of AARO within 60 days and to hand over within 180 days 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material,' with civil and criminal immunity for those who comply. Third, it disallows independent research and development funding on such material as an indirect expense unless it is surrendered. The Senate passed all of it on 27 July 2023. The enacted version, Section 7343 of P.L. 118-31, kept the funding limitation in generic form and deleted the enumerated activities, the contractor turn-in, the comprehensive list, and the immunity.
affiliations: Chairman, Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (2021-2025); Vice Chairman (2025- )
people.tierRationale: Sole author of the only text Congress has ever passed that legislates a contractor inventory of 'non-earth origin' material with immunity for surrender.

people.label: Daniel P. Sheehan
people.sub: Constitutional attorney; lobbied the FY2024 NDAA conference
people.narrative: Sheehan is the named source for what happened inside the FY2024 conference. A constitutional lawyer with a long history in national-security litigation, he worked the UAPDA directly on Capitol Hill and afterwards stated on the record that Turner moved first against two specific provisions — the eminent domain clause and the Review Board's subpoena power — and demanded both be struck. His account is Tier 2: it is attributed, named and contemporaneous, and it is corroborated by the enacted text, which is missing exactly those two things and nothing adjacent to them. Sheehan's value on this board is that he converts an anonymous legislative outcome into an attributable act. The conference produced no public document identifying who struck what; without a participant willing to name names, the removal would read as ordinary attrition rather than as a targeted excision of the two mechanisms that could have reached privately held material.

people.label: David Charles Grusch
people.sub: Former NGA/NRO officer; ICIG complainant; the proximate cause of the UAPDA
people.narrative: Grusch is why this legislation exists in the form it does. His allegations, published on 5 June 2023 and delivered under oath to the House Oversight Committee on 26 July 2023, are that a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme exists and has been concealed from Congress, including by moving material to defence contractors. The UAPDA was filed thirty-eight days after the first publication and its drafting shows the imprint: it defines 'legacy program' to reach 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin,' it defines 'controlling authority' to include any 'commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession' of such material, and its eminent domain clause exists for no other purpose than to reach material held outside the Government. Warner's parallel Section 1102 goes at the same target from the funding side, ordering contractors to surrender a 'comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.' Both texts passed the Senate. Both enforcement mechanisms were removed in conference. The Senate wrote the statutory definitions to fit Grusch's allegations and the conference deleted the tools that would have tested them.

entities.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023
entities.sub: Division G, S. 2226 as passed by the Senate
entities.desc: The UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 is the only text ever passed by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the assumption that recovered non-human technology and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held, in part, by private entities. It began as S.Amdt. 797, submitted by Senator Schumer on 13 July 2023 for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and printed in the Congressional Record at 169 Cong. Rec. S2953-S2959. It travelled into the engrossed Senate bill as Division G, Sections 9001 through 9015, and the Senate passed it on 27 July 2023. Section 9002 states the premise in statutory findings: that legislation is necessary 'because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified,' in part because of Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an 'over-broad interpretation of transclassified foreign nuclear information.' Section 9003 defines 'non-human intelligence' as 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin,' defines 'legacy program' to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment, and defines 'controlling authority' to include any private entity in physical possession of such material. Sections 9004 through 9006 create a Records Collection at the National Archives with a presumption of immediate disclosure. Sections 9007 through 9009 create a nine-member Review Board appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, barred from including anyone with previous or current involvement in any legacy program, empowered to order disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence for postponement, and required to produce a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan. Section 9010 orders the exercise of eminent domain. Section 9014 authorises $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024. Sections 9007 through 9011 and 9014 were removed in conference and have never been enacted.

entities.label: Section 9010(a) — Exercise of Eminent Domain
entities.sub: Statutory text passed by the Senate, 27 July 2023
entities.desc: The single most important sentence in the modern disclosure record, and a Tier 1 documented fact whose existence does not depend on believing any witness. Section 9010 of Division G of S. 2226, headed 'Disclosure of Recovered Technologies of Unknown Origin and Biological Evidence of Non-Human Intelligence,' opens: 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Subsection (b) requires that 'any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material.' Subsection (c) directs the Board to decide 'whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt.' The drafting is careful and revealing in both directions: the hedge 'should it exist' preserves deniability, while 'shall exercise' is mandatory and the taking is aimed exclusively at private holders, not at Government agencies — the Government does not need eminent domain against itself. A chamber of Congress passed this. It was then deleted, and the deletion is the fact that organises this entire domain.

entities.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board
entities.sub: Independent agency, authorised by the Senate, never constituted
entities.desc: The Review Board is the JFK Records Act transplant at the centre of the UAPDA and the thing the conference was most determined to prevent. Section 9007 establishes it 'as an independent agency' — outside the Department of Defense, outside the intelligence community, outside the armed services and intelligence committees. The President appoints nine citizens 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate,' with nominations due within 90 days of enactment and a replacement nomination required within 30 days of any Senate rejection. Nominees are drawn from recommendations by the four congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, 'established nonprofit research organizations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' and the American Historical Association. The disqualification in Section 9007(b)(4)(A) is the operative clause: members 'shall be impartial citizens, none of whom shall have had any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence.' The composition is mandated to include a national security official, a foreign service official, a scientist or engineer, an economist, a professional historian and a sociologist. Under Section 9009(c)(1) the Board must order disclosure 'in the absence of clear and convincing evidence' for postponement — reversing the ordinary classification presumption. Under Section 9010(b) recovered material must be made available to it for personal examination. The Board was removed in conference and does not exist. Nothing in enacted law performs its function: under Section 1843 of P.L. 118-31 the postponement decision is made by 'the original classification authority.'

entities.label: Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan
entities.sub: Sec. 9009(c)(3) — mandated managed-release schedule, never produced
entities.desc: The Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan is the UAPDA's answer to the objection that disclosure must be managed rather than instantaneous, and it is the concept the disclosure movement has since adopted as its central demand. Under Section 9009(c)(3) the Review Board would have been required to create and transmit to the President, the Archivist, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the House Oversight and Accountability Committee a plan with a classified appendix covering every record, every piece of information, and every item of 'recovered technologies of unknown origin, and biological evidence for non-human intelligence' whose disclosure was postponed. The plan had to contain a justification of each postponement and 'a benchmark-driven plan... recommending precise requirements for periodic review, downgrading, and declassification as well as the exact time or specified occurrence following which each postponed item may be appropriately disclosed to the public.' In other words: nothing could be withheld indefinitely, and every withholding had to carry a dated exit. Section 9009(b)(6) required the Board to brief AARO on the Plan before terminating, and Section 9013(b)(2) required AARO to carry the Plan's logic forward into standing declassification guidance for records created after the Board wound up. All of it was removed. No Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan exists, and no enacted provision requires one.

The Act signed on 22 December 2023 contains, in place of Division G, a three-section Subtitle C of Title XVIII: Sec. 1841, the Records Collection at the National Archives; Sec. 1842, review and transmission by heads of Government offices within 300 days; and Sec. 1843, grounds for postponement. entities.label: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C — Secs. 1841-1843 (what survived)
entities.sub: Enacted UAP records regime, 22 December 2023
entities.desc: What Congress actually enacted is a records-transfer statute with the enforcement removed. Sec. 1841 orders the Archivist to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection, requires physical integrity and original provenance to be preserved, requires public availability within 30 days of transmission and online within 180 days thereafter, and assigns continuing oversight to six committees. Sec. 1842 bars destruction, alteration or mutilation of any UAP record, bars withholding or reclassification of anything already public, bars withholding of records created outside the Federal Government, and gives agency heads 300 days to review and organise. Sec. 1843 is where it fails. Postponement may be ordered where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of harm — the clear and convincing standard survives, but the person applying it is the classifier rather than an independent board, which converts a check into a self-certification. Senior Agency Officials may unilaterally withdraw records from the Collection on a determination that they are both unrelated to UAP and properly classified, needing only to notify Congress 60 days beforehand. Where disclosure is postponed the agency head must notify congressional leadership within 15 days with a reason. There is no appeal, no de novo review, no subpoena and no mechanism reaching material rather than paper.

It opens with a sense of Congress that the Federal Government 'must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes' — a statement that the Government has previously handed exotic technology to industry. It then cuts off all funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access not 'formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified' to Congress and the AARO Director, enumerating six categories including personnel whose mission is 'capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft,' analysis to determine 'material composition, method of manufacture, origin,' 'reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology,' and 'any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Subsection (d) then requires any current or former Federal contractor holding such material to notify the AARO Director within 60 days and, within 180 days, to make available all of it plus 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.' Subsection (e) grants full civil and criminal immunity to those who comply. Subsection (f) disallows independent research and development funding on such material as an indirect expense unless it is surrendered, effective 60 days after enactment and applicable to money appropriated before as well as after. The Senate passed all of this on 27 July 2023.

entities.desc: Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, signed 27 December 2021, is the statutory root of the entire modern apparatus. It directed the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to establish within 180 days an office inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense or a joint DoD/ODNI organisation to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. Its enumerated duties reach beyond analysis into governance: synchronising and standardising collection and reporting 'including adverse physiological effects' across DoD and the intelligence community, forcing incident reports into a centralised repository, evaluating links to adversary and non-state actors, and coordinating with the FAA, NASA, DHS, NOAA and the Department of Energy. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, and every subsequent UAP provision — Sec. 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA, Sec. 1687 and Sec. 7343 of the FY2024 NDAA, Sec. 6801 of the IAA FY2025, and Secs. 1671-1673 of the FY2026 NDAA — cross-references it. It was restated in full by Sec. 6802 of the IAA FY2023, which named the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, set the Director reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI, entitled ten named intelligence elements to place detailees inside it, and added subsection (j), the Historical Record Report on the United States Government's dealings with UAP built from intelligence community records, oral histories and interviews of current and former officials.

entities.label: FY2023 NDAA Sec. 1673 (P.L. 117-263; 50 U.S.C. 3373b)
entities.sub: Authorized reporting mechanism and whistleblower protection
entities.desc: Section 1673 is the provision that makes the legacy programme a matter of enacted federal law rather than allegation, and it is routinely underrated. It orders the Secretary of Defense, through the head of AARO, to establish a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of 'any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.' Congress does not legislate reporting channels for categories of programme it believes do not exist. The protections are unusually strong: an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure,' is deemed to comply with Executive Order 13526 and with chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act, and 'is not a violation of section 798 of title 18' or any other disclosure statute. Reprisal — including 'the revocation or suspension of security clearances, or termination of employment' — is prohibited. Subsection (b)(3) then orders DoD, ODNI, DHS, other supporting agencies and Federal contractors that 'have supported or are supporting such activities and programs' to conduct comprehensive searches of all records relating to nondisclosure orders on these subjects and deliver copies to AARO, which must make them accessible to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership. This is a statutory census of the gag orders. It has never been reported as completed.

entities.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection (NARA Record Group 615)
entities.sub: National Archives collection created under Secs. 1841-1843
entities.desc: RG 615 is the only thing the UAPDA fight actually built. Established under Sections 1841-1843 of P.L. 118-31, it is a dedicated National Archives record group into which every Federal agency is required to transmit copies of its UAP records, with the Archivist obliged to preserve physical integrity and original provenance, publish a subject guidebook and index, make records available for inspection within 30 days of transmission and online within a further 180 days, and maintain a central directory of identification aids. The National Security Program Office at NARA, working with the Information Security Oversight Office, is required to run a security programme for the postponed, still-classified portion. NARA issued guidance to agencies on transferring publicly releasable UAP records in April 2025 — sixteen months after enactment and roughly six months after the statutory 300-day agency review deadline of 17 October 2024 had already passed — and states that records will be added 'on an ongoing, rolling basis as they are received from federal agencies.' The collection is the measurable test of the enacted statute: it exists, it is real, and its rate of fill is the honest metric for whether Sections 1841-1843 accomplish anything without the Review Board that was supposed to force them.

P.L. 119-60, approved 18 December 2025, contains a Subtitle E of Title XVI headed 'Matters Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena' with three sections. Sec. 1671 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(l) to require that AARO's briefings include details of any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or United States Northern Command, with the first such briefing required to reach back over intercepts 'that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004' — Congress choosing the year of the Nimitz encounters as its retroactive floor. Sec. 1672 repeals Sec. 413 of the IAA FY2022, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373a, and rewrites the data-availability clause so that intelligence and DoD components must make UAP data available 'immediately' to AARO. Sec. 1673 orders the AARO Director within 180 days to make an accounting of the security classification guides applying to UAP reporting and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix — a direct probe at the classification architecture itself. They were not renewed in FY2025 and were not renewed here, so the statutory bar on funding undisclosed UAP special access programmes has now lapsed for two consecutive authorisation cycles. The Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2026 that rides in Division F contains no UAP provisions at all.

entities.sub: The surviving teeth, lapsed after FY2024
entities.desc: Section 1687 is the one enacted provision that reaches at the concealment itself rather than at the paperwork. It bars any funds authorised by the FY2024 NDAA from being obligated or expended 'in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b), noted as 50 U.S.C. 3373 note, then bars UAP-related independent research and development from being allowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to those same committees — a direct strike at the mechanism by which contractor-held work can be paid for out of overhead without appearing as a Government programme. Its limitation is structural: it restricts funds 'authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act,' meaning the FY2024 Act only. It was not re-enacted in the FY2025 NDAA or the FY2026 NDAA, neither of which contains the phrase 'special access or restricted access'. The statutory bar therefore covered one fiscal year and has now been absent for two.

timeline.label: Sec. 1683 enacted
timeline.text: The FY2022 NDAA is signed as P.L. 117-81. Section 1683, Gillibrand's provision, orders a permanent UAP office stood up within 180 days and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373.

timeline.label: Harry Reid dies
timeline.text: Reid dies one day after the enactment of the statute that institutionalises the subject he had funded through leadership discretion in 2008.

timeline.label: AARO named; Historical Record Report ordered
timeline.text: P.L. 117-263 carries IAA FY2023 Sec. 6802, restating Sec. 1683 to name the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, and Sec. 1673, creating the authorized reporting channel that voids nondisclosure agreements.

timeline.label: Sixteen senators demand full AARO funding
timeline.text: Gillibrand and Rubio lead fourteen colleagues insisting AARO receive the amount in the classified attachment, arguing the office offers 'increased transparency to the American people.'

timeline.label: Grusch allegations published
timeline.text: Allegations of a concealed multi-decade crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering programme, including transfer of material to defence contractors, enter the public record.

timeline.label: S. 2226 introduced
timeline.text: Chairman Jack Reed introduces the FY2024 NDAA, the vehicle that will carry both UAP regimes.

timeline.label: S.Amdt. 797 filed
timeline.text: Schumer submits the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 with Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich; the text prints at 169 Cong. Rec. S2953-S2959. Warner files S.Amdt. 666, the IAA carrying the contractor turn-in, the same day.

timeline.label: House Oversight hearing
timeline.text: Grusch testifies under oath, thirteen days after the amendment premised on his allegations is filed.

timeline.label: Senate passes both regimes
timeline.text: S. 2226 passes the Senate carrying Division G, Secs. 9001-9015 including the eminent domain command, and Division M Sec. 1102, the contractor turn-in with immunity.

timeline.label: Turner disparages the testimony
timeline.text: The HPSCI chairman says the striking thing about the hearing was that 'repeatedly over and over again, the whistleblowers had to say, actually, I don't have any knowledge.'

timeline.label: Turner and Rogers named
timeline.text: Reporting identifies Turner and Rogers as leading the effort to eliminate or alter the Act, with McConnell and Speaker Johnson supporting; Sheehan states Turner demanded the eminent domain provision and the subpoena power be struck.

timeline.label: Senate accepts the gutting in silence
timeline.text: The Senate's final consideration of the FY2024 NDAA produces no transcribed remarks containing the word 'anomalous'; no member objects aloud to the removal of the division the chamber had passed.

timeline.label: The stripping is enacted
timeline.text: P.L. 118-31 is signed. Fifteen sections become three. The Review Board, the eminent domain clause, the Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, the $20,000,000 authorization, the contractor turn-in and the immunity grant are all gone. Sec. 7343 is left referring to an instruction it no longer identifies.

timeline.label: UAPDA refiled as SA 2610
timeline.text: Rounds, for himself and Schumer, refiles the complete Act against the FY2025 NDAA with the eminent domain command unchanged. It is ordered to lie on the table and never called up.

timeline.label: Agency review deadline expires
timeline.text: The 300-day deadline in Sec. 1842(c)(1) for every Government office to review, identify and organise its UAP records passes.

timeline.label: FY2025 enacted with no disclosure regime
timeline.text: P.L. 118-159 contains only a GAO review of AARO and a sunset on audit briefings. The FY2024 funding bar on undisclosed UAP special access programmes is not renewed.

timeline.label: Rubio leaves the Senate
timeline.text: The SSCI Vice Chairman who cosponsored the eminent domain text departs on confirmation as Secretary of State, removing the disclosure coalition's most senior intelligence-committee Republican.

timeline.label: NARA issues transfer guidance
timeline.text: Sixteen months after enactment and roughly six months after the statutory agency deadline, the National Archives issues guidance on transferring publicly releasable UAP records into Record Group 615.

timeline.label: Gillibrand's FY2026 claim
timeline.text: Gillibrand announces her FY2026 defense bill wins; her only UAP item is 'language to update congressional briefing requirements for UAP.'

timeline.label: No open amendment process
timeline.text: The FY2026 NDAA is moved with seventeen amendments in total; the only Senate floor amendment proposed is a leadership amendment by Senator Thune 'to improve the bill.' There is no process in which the UAPDA could be offered.

timeline.label: FY2026 enacted; funding bar lapses again
timeline.text: P.L. 119-60 carries a three-section housekeeping subtitle: intercept briefings back to 2004, repeal of a duplicative report, and an accounting of classification guides. No Review Board, no eminent domain, and for the second consecutive year no funding bar on undisclosed UAP special access programmes.

timeline.label: Department of War releases UAP files
timeline.text: The administration announces a release of UAP files. Gillibrand, author of the surviving statute, calls it 'another important step' and says she will fight to ensure the administration 'finally meets its legal obligation' — nineteen months after the deadline.

timeline.label: FY2027 NDAA reported with no UAP provisions
timeline.text: S. 4784, Report No. 119-127, is reported by the Armed Services Committee containing zero occurrences of 'unidentified', 'UAP' or a citation to 50 U.S.C. 3373. Second consecutive cycle in which the subject is absent from the Senate base text.

timeline.label: Rounds's markup wins contain no UAP item
timeline.text: Rounds announces roughly forty provisions he secured in the FY2027 committee markup. None concerns unidentified anomalous phenomena.

timeline.label: Rounds announces a fourth attempt
timeline.text: At the 2026 Disclosure Symposium Rounds says he is 'once again cosponsoring' the UAP Disclosure Act as an amendment to this year's NDAA — nine days after the committee reported a bill with nothing in it to amend.

uapda-sec-9010-eminent-domain.desc:
Full text as passed by the Senate, 27 July 2023, S. 2226 Division G:

SEC. 9010. DISCLOSURE OF RECOVERED TECHNOLOGIES OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN AND BIOLOGICAL EVIDENCE OF NON-HUMAN INTELLIGENCE.
(a) Exercise of Eminent Domain.--The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.
(b) Availability to Review Board.--Any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material and in a timely manner conducive to the objectives of the Review Board in accordance with the requirements of this division.
(c) Actions of Review Board.--In carrying out subsection (b), the Review Board shall consider and render decisions-- (1) whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt; (2) whether recovered technologies of unknown origin, biological evidence of non-human intelligence, or a particular subset of material qualifies for postponement of disclosure under this division...

uapda-2023.desc:
Key statutory definitions as passed by the Senate (Sec. 9003):

(5) 'controlling authority' means any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.

(11) 'legacy program' means all Federal, State, and local government, commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.

(13) 'non-human intelligence' means any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.

(2) 'close observer' means anyone who has come into close proximity to unidentified anomalous phenomena or non-human intelligence.

The Sec. 9003(23) definition of a 'unidentified anomalous phenomena record' reaches twenty-four categories of holder, expressly including the Department of Defense 'and its progenitors, the Department of War and the Department of the Navy'; the Air Force Office of Special Investigations by name; the Department of Energy 'and its progenitors, the Manhattan Project, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Energy Research and Development Administration'; the CIA 'and its progenitor, the Office of Strategic Services'; the NRO, DIA, NSA, NGA, NASA, FBI, FAA, NOAA and the Library of Congress; and, at subparagraph (X), 'any private sector person or entity formerly or currently under contract or some other agreement with the Federal Government.'

iaa-fy2024-sec-1102.desc:
Senate-passed IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102(d), verbatim:

'(d) Notification and Reporting.--Any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access shall-- (1) not later than 60 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, notify the Director of such possession; and (2) not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, make available to the Director for assessment, analysis, and inspection-- (A) all such material and information; and (B) a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.'

And Sec. 1102(e): 'No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving material or information described in subsection (d) if that person complies with the notification and reporting provisions described in such subsection.'

None of this appears in the enacted Sec. 7343 of P.L. 118-31.

gaps: No conference document, joint explanatory statement annex, or committee record has been released identifying which members struck Secs. 9007-9011 and 9014 from the FY2024 NDAA, or which struck subsections (b), (d), (e) and (g) from IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102. The attribution to Turner and Rogers rests on named-participant testimony and journalism, not on a signed record. A targeted FOIA or committee-records request is the obvious next step.

Rubio's widely quoted statement that people with 'very high clearances and high positions within our government' have made firsthand claims could not be sourced to a verifiable primary URL from this workstation. The NewsNation interview is real and repeatedly cited; the citation needs to be pinned before the quote is used.

No compliance data exists on Sec. 1842. How many agencies met the 17 October 2024 deadline, how many records each transmitted, and how many postponements were certified under Sec. 1843(a) are all unknown. NARA's RG 615 accession record and the Sec. 1843(c) 15-day congressional postponement notifications would answer this.

The Sec. 1673(b)(3) census of UAP nondisclosure orders — comprehensive searches by DoD, ODNI, DHS and contractors, with copies delivered to AARO and made accessible to Congress — has no public completion record. This is the single highest-value unretrieved document set in the domain.
The GAO review of AARO commissioned by Sec. 6801 of the IAA FY2025 has a deadline set only 'in a timeframe mutually agreed upon.' Whether it has been delivered, and in what form, is unknown.
The contents and scope of the Department of War's 8 May 2026 UAP file release are undetermined; war.gov blocks automated retrieval and Gillibrand's statement does not enumerate what was released.
The Sec. 1673 accounting of UAP security classification guides required by the FY2026 NDAA within 180 days of 18 December 2025 fell due around 16 June 2026. No public evidence of delivery was found.

Whether Rounds actually filed the announced 2026 UAPDA amendment to S. 4784, and under what amendment number, is not yet in the bill status record; as of the data available the FY2027 NDAA had only reached a motion to proceed on 14 July 2026.
Speaker Mike Johnson's role is named in a single journalistic source and is not otherwise documented; he is referenced in claims here but not given a node.
